metadata.name: WordPress Core Execution Tests - Plugin Lifecycle
metadata.description: Plugin artifact tasks for WordPress plugin activation, deactivation, uninstall, dependencies, upgrades and data migrations, and plugin screen integration

tests.prompt: Build a small WordPress plugin that looks after its own stored settings across its lifecycle. When the plugin is activated it stores the option wpbp_reader_settings with its defaults: version 2, per_page 10 and show_covers true, without overwriting settings that are already there. Every time WordPress finishes loading plugins the plugin checks the stored settings and upgrades anything left behind by its version 1, which stored a single perPage entry: the reader's page size is carried over, the missing default is filled in and the current version is stamped. The upgrade must run only when the stored settings are older than the current version, and each run must add one to the option wpbp_reader_upgrades. The plugin must also tell WordPress which function to call to clean up its options when the plugin is deleted.
tests.expected_behavior: The main plugin file calls `register_activation_hook( __FILE__, ... )` with a seeding callback, hooks a version-gated upgrade routine to `plugins_loaded`, and calls `register_uninstall_hook( __FILE__, ... )` with a named function or static method (a closure is refused by core). Runtime validation fires the discovered `activate_wp-bench-candidate-*` action, then sets a version 1 payload and fires `plugins_loaded` twice to prove the upgrade is version gated and counted once, then checks that current settings are left alone and that the uninstall callback is recorded in the `uninstall_plugins` option.
requirements: Register the activation routine so WordPress runs it on activation of this plugin file
Seed the defaults only when no settings are stored yet
Attach the upgrade check to the plugins_loaded action with add_action, even though this plugin file is loaded after the site has already fired plugins_loaded
Upgrade only settings older than the current version, keeping the stored page size, and add one to wpbp_reader_upgrades on each upgrade
Register an uninstall callback that is a named function or a static method rather than a closure

reference_files.wpbp-reader.php:
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: WPBP Reader
 * Description: Reader settings with activation, upgrade and uninstall handling.
 * Version: 2.0.0
 */

if ( ! defined( 'WPBP_READER_VERSION' ) ) {
	define( 'WPBP_READER_VERSION', 2 );
}

function wpbp_reader_default_settings(): array {
	return array(
		'version'     => WPBP_READER_VERSION,
		'per_page'    => 10,
		'show_covers' => true,
	);
}

function wpbp_reader_activate(): void {
	if ( false === get_option( 'wpbp_reader_settings', false ) ) {
		add_option( 'wpbp_reader_settings', wpbp_reader_default_settings() );
	}
}
register_activation_hook( __FILE__, 'wpbp_reader_activate' );

function wpbp_reader_maybe_upgrade(): void {
	$settings = get_option( 'wpbp_reader_settings' );

	if ( ! is_array( $settings ) ) {
		return;
	}

	$version = isset( $settings['version'] ) ? (int) $settings['version'] : 1;

	if ( $version >= WPBP_READER_VERSION ) {
		return;
	}

	$upgraded = wpbp_reader_default_settings();

	if ( isset( $settings['perPage'] ) ) {
		$upgraded['per_page'] = (int) $settings['perPage'];
	} elseif ( isset( $settings['per_page'] ) ) {
		$upgraded['per_page'] = (int) $settings['per_page'];
	}

	if ( isset( $settings['show_covers'] ) ) {
		$upgraded['show_covers'] = (bool) $settings['show_covers'];
	}

	update_option( 'wpbp_reader_settings', $upgraded );
	update_option( 'wpbp_reader_upgrades', (int) get_option( 'wpbp_reader_upgrades', 0 ) + 1 );
}
add_action( 'plugins_loaded', 'wpbp_reader_maybe_upgrade' );

function wpbp_reader_uninstall(): void {
	delete_option( 'wpbp_reader_settings' );
	delete_option( 'wpbp_reader_upgrades' );
}
register_uninstall_hook( __FILE__, 'wpbp_reader_uninstall' );

tests.prompt: Build a small WordPress plugin that improves its own row on the Plugins screen. Its list of action links gains a 'Settings' link, ahead of the links WordPress already offers there, pointing at this site's admin page options-general.php?page=wpbp-reader. The meta line under its description gains a 'Docs' link to https://example.org/wpbp-reader-docs, after the entries WordPress already puts there. Both additions must apply to this plugin's row only, and must work no matter which directory the plugin is installed in.
tests.expected_behavior: The plugin builds its own file name with `plugin_basename( __FILE__ )` and uses it both for the plugin-specific action links filter (`plugin_action_links_{$file}`) and for the `$plugin_file` comparison inside the shared `plugin_row_meta` filter, prepending the settings anchor with `admin_url()` and appending the docs anchor. Runtime validation discovers the registered `plugin_action_links_wp-bench-candidate-*` hook, applies it with a deactivate link in place, and applies `plugin_row_meta` for the plugin itself and for an unrelated plugin file.
requirements: Derive the plugin's own file name at runtime rather than hard-coding a directory
Add the Settings link through the filter WordPress offers for this plugin's own action links, ahead of the existing links, and keep them
Point the Settings link at this site's admin URL for options-general.php?page=wpbp-reader
Append a Docs link to https://example.org/wpbp-reader-docs to this plugin's row meta, keeping the entries already there
Leave other plugins' action links and row meta untouched

tests.prompt: Build a WordPress plugin, WPBP Digest, that emails a daily digest. When it is activated it schedules its daily event wpbp_digest_send (only once, even if it is activated again) and stores its settings in the option wpbp_digest_settings with the default array( 'hour' => 8 ), unless settings are already stored. While it runs it also queues one-off retry events on the hook wpbp_digest_retry, each carrying a recipient's user ID as its only argument, keeps the last digest in the transient wpbp_digest_cache, and stores each user's opt-out flag in the user meta wpbp_digest_optout. Deactivating the plugin must leave no scheduled work behind (the daily event and every queued retry, whatever its argument) and must drop the cached digest, but it must keep the settings and the users' opt-outs so that reactivating the plugin restores them. Deleting the plugin, which WordPress only allows once it is deactivated, must remove the data it kept: its settings and the opt-out flag of every user. Data that belongs to other plugins must survive both.
tests.expected_behavior: The main file calls `register_activation_hook( __FILE__, ... )` with a callback that schedules `wpbp_digest_send` daily behind a `wp_next_scheduled()` guard and seeds the settings with `add_option()`, and `register_deactivation_hook( __FILE__, ... )` with a callback that removes every `wpbp_digest_send` and `wpbp_digest_retry` event (`wp_unschedule_hook()`, or `wp_clear_scheduled_hook()` once per argument set; `wp_clear_scheduled_hook( 'wpbp_digest_retry' )` alone only clears events scheduled without arguments) and deletes the transient, leaving options and user meta alone. Deletion is handled by an `uninstall.php` guarded by `WP_UNINSTALL_PLUGIN` or by `register_uninstall_hook()` with a named callback, deleting the option and the user meta for all users (for example `delete_metadata( 'user', 0, 'wpbp_digest_optout', '', true )`) without wildcards that reach other plugins' data. Runtime validation fires the discovered `activate_` and `deactivate_` hooks for the candidate plugin, then calls core's `uninstall_plugin()` for its basename, with another plugin's option, transient, daily event and user meta in place.
requirements: Schedule wpbp_digest_send as a daily event on activation, never twice, and seed wpbp_digest_settings only when nothing is stored
On deactivation remove the daily event and every wpbp_digest_retry event whatever its argument, and delete the wpbp_digest_cache transient
Keep wpbp_digest_settings and the wpbp_digest_optout user meta on deactivation
On deletion (uninstall.php or an uninstall hook) remove wpbp_digest_settings and wpbp_digest_optout for every user
Leave other plugins' options, transients, scheduled events and user meta untouched

reference_files.wpbp-digest.php:
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: WPBP Digest
 * Description: Emails a daily digest.
 * Version: 1.0.0
 */

function wpbp_digest_activate(): void {
	if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'wpbp_digest_send' ) ) {
		wp_schedule_event( time() + HOUR_IN_SECONDS, 'daily', 'wpbp_digest_send' );
	}

	add_option( 'wpbp_digest_settings', array( 'hour' => 8 ) );
}
register_activation_hook( __FILE__, 'wpbp_digest_activate' );

function wpbp_digest_deactivate(): void {
	wp_unschedule_hook( 'wpbp_digest_send' );
	wp_unschedule_hook( 'wpbp_digest_retry' );
	delete_transient( 'wpbp_digest_cache' );
}
register_deactivation_hook( __FILE__, 'wpbp_digest_deactivate' );

<?php
/**
 * Removes WPBP Digest data when the plugin is deleted.
 */

if ( ! defined( 'WP_UNINSTALL_PLUGIN' ) ) {
	exit;
}

delete_option( 'wpbp_digest_settings' );
delete_metadata( 'user', 0, 'wpbp_digest_optout', '', true );

tests.prompt: Build WPBP Shop Extras, an add-on for the WPBP Shop plugin, whose WordPress.org slug is wpbp-shop. The add-on's plugin header must name it WPBP Shop Extras, give version 1.3.0 and the text domain wpbp-shop-extras, and declare that it needs WordPress 6.8 or later, PHP 8.1 or later and the wpbp-shop plugin, so that WordPress itself enforces those requirements. WPBP Shop announces itself while plugins are loading by firing the action wpbp_shop_loaded with its version string as the only argument. Once all plugins have loaded, the add-on starts only if WPBP Shop announced version 2.4.0 or later; starting means filtering wpbp_shop_price (a float) to add 10% tax, rounded to two decimals. If WPBP Shop is missing or older, prices must be left alone and users who can activate plugins see an error admin notice reading 'WPBP Shop Extras needs WPBP Shop 2.4.0 or later.'

reference_files.wpbp-shop-extras.php:
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: WPBP Shop Extras
 * Description: Adds tax handling to WPBP Shop.
 * Version: 1.3.0
 * Requires at least: 6.8
 * Requires PHP: 8.1
 * Requires Plugins: wpbp-shop
 * Text Domain: wpbp-shop-extras
 */

const WPBP_SHOP_EXTRAS_MIN_SHOP = '2.4.0';

function wpbp_shop_extras_shop_version( ?string $announced = null ): ?string {
	static $version = null;

	if ( null !== $announced ) {
		$version = $announced;
	}

	return $version;
}

add_action(
	'wpbp_shop_loaded',
	static function ( $version ): void {
		wpbp_shop_extras_shop_version( (string) $version );
	}
);

function wpbp_shop_extras_boot(): void {
	$version = wpbp_shop_extras_shop_version();

	if ( null === $version || version_compare( $version, WPBP_SHOP_EXTRAS_MIN_SHOP, '<' ) ) {
		add_action( 'admin_notices', 'wpbp_shop_extras_missing_notice' );
		return;
	}

	add_filter( 'wpbp_shop_price', 'wpbp_shop_extras_add_tax' );
}
add_action( 'plugins_loaded', 'wpbp_shop_extras_boot', 20 );

function wpbp_shop_extras_add_tax( $price ): float {
	return round( (float) $price * 1.1, 2 );
}

function wpbp_shop_extras_missing_notice(): void {
	if ( ! current_user_can( 'activate_plugins' ) ) {
		return;
	}

	wp_admin_notice(
		esc_html__( 'WPBP Shop Extras needs WPBP Shop 2.4.0 or later.', 'wpbp-shop-extras' ),
		array( 'type' => 'error' )
	);
}

tests.prompt: WPBP Ratings 2.0 changes how it stores ratings. Version 1 kept a post's rating in the post meta _wpbp_rating as a score out of 10, such as '7'. Version 2 keeps the post meta wpbp_stars, a whole score out of 5 (half the old score with halves rounded up, so 7 becomes 4), and no longer keeps _wpbp_rating. The plugin records the format of the site's data in the option wpbp_ratings_db_version: sites still holding version 1 data have '1', and it must read '2' once every rating has been converted. Sites can have many thousands of rated posts, so the conversion must never run in a single request. Build the plugin so that, when WordPress finishes loading plugins on a site with version 1 data, it queues the one-off cron event wpbp_ratings_migrate to run as soon as possible, unless one is already queued. Each run of that event converts the next 50 posts that still need converting (fewer only when fewer remain) and queues the next run while any remain; the run that finishes the work sets the data version to '2' and queues nothing more. Posts without a rating must not gain one.
tests.expected_behavior: A `plugins_loaded` callback compares the stored `wpbp_ratings_db_version` with the current version and, when it is older, calls `wp_schedule_single_event( time(), 'wpbp_ratings_migrate' )` behind a `wp_next_scheduled()` guard without converting anything itself. The `wpbp_ratings_migrate` callback queries 50 post IDs that still have `_wpbp_rating` (for example `get_posts()` with `meta_key`, `fields => 'ids'`, `posts_per_page => 50`), writes `wpbp_stars` as `ceil( score / 2 )` (integer division or truncation turns 7 into 3) and deletes `_wpbp_rating` so the next query moves on, then either queues the next single event or, when nothing is left, updates the version option. Runtime validation creates 70 rated and 3 unrated posts, fires the plugin's `plugins_loaded` callbacks twice, then runs the queued event the way WP-Cron does (unschedule, then `do_action_ref_array()`) and checks 50 conversions, then the remaining 20 with every value, the version stamp and an empty queue.
requirements: On plugins_loaded, queue a single wpbp_ratings_migrate event when the data version is older than 2 and none is queued, without converting posts
Convert exactly the next 50 posts per run, fewer only on the last run
Store wpbp_stars as the old score halved and rounded up, and delete _wpbp_rating from converted posts
Queue the next run while unconverted posts remain; otherwise set wpbp_ratings_db_version to '2' and queue nothing
Leave posts without a rating unchanged

<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: WPBP Ratings
 * Description: Star ratings for posts.
 * Version: 2.0.0
 */

const WPBP_RATINGS_DB_VERSION = '2';
const WPBP_RATINGS_BATCH_SIZE = 50;

function wpbp_ratings_maybe_migrate(): void {
	$stored = get_option( 'wpbp_ratings_db_version' );

	if ( false === $stored || version_compare( (string) $stored, WPBP_RATINGS_DB_VERSION, '>=' ) ) {
		return;
	}

	if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'wpbp_ratings_migrate' ) ) {
		wp_schedule_single_event( time(), 'wpbp_ratings_migrate' );
	}
}
add_action( 'plugins_loaded', 'wpbp_ratings_maybe_migrate' );

function wpbp_ratings_pending( int $limit ): array {
	return get_posts(
		array(
			'post_type'      => 'any',
			'post_status'    => 'any',
			'meta_key'       => '_wpbp_rating',
			'fields'         => 'ids',
			'posts_per_page' => $limit,
			'orderby'        => 'ID',
			'order'          => 'ASC',
			'no_found_rows'  => true,
		)
	);
}

function wpbp_ratings_migrate_batch(): void {
	foreach ( wpbp_ratings_pending( WPBP_RATINGS_BATCH_SIZE ) as $post_id ) {
		$score = (int) get_post_meta( $post_id, '_wpbp_rating', true );

		update_post_meta( $post_id, 'wpbp_stars', (int) ceil( $score / 2 ) );
		delete_post_meta( $post_id, '_wpbp_rating' );
	}

	if ( array() !== wpbp_ratings_pending( 1 ) ) {
		wp_schedule_single_event( time(), 'wpbp_ratings_migrate' );
		return;
	}

	update_option( 'wpbp_ratings_db_version', WPBP_RATINGS_DB_VERSION );
}
add_action( 'wpbp_ratings_migrate', 'wpbp_ratings_migrate_batch' );
